To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the discourses of the market and the child are not compatible, and the discourses of early childhood education are contradictory.

the early years sector is not free market as policy has created a discursive truth to secure initial pump priming investments, but that the sustainability of the sector is in question, and the tension between the entrepreneurial and romantic discourses of early childhood education is due to a rejection, in the latter, of a commodity view.

the discursive constructions of early childhood education are contradictory, and that there is a tension between the romanticisation of early childhood education as a place where children are valued as individuals, and the entrepreneurial discourse that is being constructed by government.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the construction of early childhood and care services and how these are negotiated by providers and policy makers.

the ways in which early childhood education and childcare services are constructed and how the constructions are used to justify the provision of services and the ways in which the services are delivered.
understanding how the early childhood education and carers' experiences of the mixed economy are shaped and mediated by discourses and the tensions between them.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is no one discourse that can be applied to all providers of early childhood education, care and support services, as there are many different types of provider, many different types of provision and many different types of children and families.
the construction of early childhood services is complex and contested.

there is a need for a new construction of early childhood services that recognises that children are both consumers and commodities, but that the construction must be from within the sector and must not obscure the voice and needs of the child.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the discursive constructions of early childhood education, and early childhood educators, are not only important in terms of the ways in which they shape the provision of services and the nature of the work, but also the ways in which these discourses are used to shape the lives of children.

the early childhood education and Care sector is not yet ready for the entrepreneurial discourse, but that the romanticisation of early childhood is not sustainable in the longer term. (author abstract)
we are interested in the ways that early childhood education and childcare services are conceptualised and how these conceptualisations are constructed and maintained.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the discursive construction of the early childhood education and carer as an entrepreneur, whilst a useful tool in the short term, will be unsustainable in the long term as it will fail to recognise and respond to the needs of the children, families, communities and the workforce.
we need to move away from the idea that early childhood education and carers are not entrepreneurs.
the construction of the sector needs to move beyond the romanticised view of the child, childhood and early education and care services to one that acknowledges the child as consumer.
